featured_reviews.review_text:
Khilafat movement, force that arose in India in the early 20th century as a result of Muslim fears for the integrityof Islam. These fears were aroused by Italian (1911) and Balkan (1912–13) attacks on Turkey—whose sultan, as caliph, was the religious head of the worldwide Muslim community—and by Turkish defeats in World War I. They were intensified by the Treaty of Sèvres (August 1920), which not only detached all non-Turkish regions from the empire but also gave parts of the Turkish homeland to Greece and other non-Muslim powers.
A campaign in defense of the caliph was launched, led in India by the brothers Shaukat and Muḥammad ʿAlī and by Abul Kalam Azad. The leaders joined forces with Mahatma Gandhi’s noncooperation movementfor Indian freedom, promising nonviolence in return for his support of the Khilafat movement. In 1920 the latter movement was marred by the ḥijrat, or exodus, from India to Afghanistan of about 18,000 Muslim peasants, who felt that India was an apostate land. It was also tarnished by the Muslim Moplah rebellion in south India (Malabar) in 1921, the excesses of which deeply stirred Hindu India. Gandhi’s suspension of his movement and his arrest in March 1922 weakened the Khilafat movement still further. It was further undermined when Mustafa KemalAtatürk drove the Greeks from western Asia Minor in 1922 and deposed the Turkish sultan in the same year; it finally collapsed when he abolished the caliphate altogether in 1924.

featured_reviews.name: Namrata Nayar
featured_reviews.review_text:
What should have been a review has become a eulogy, as I was just informed that Dr. Sampat is no more.

A great principal isn’t just a leader; they are a force. They shape minds, build character, and leave a mark so deep that even years later, their words echo in your heart.

Dr. Urmi Sampat was that kind of principal. She wasn’t just an educator,she was an institution.

I still remember my first day at H.J. College. She stood at the gate in a crisp cream saree, radiating authority yet warmth. “What’s your name?” she asked. “Namrata  , and I’m am going to be the topper this year,” I replied with pride. She just laughed and said, “Go and sit yourself inside.” That was Dr. Sampat, no fuss, no unnecessary praise, just straight to the point. But in that moment, she acknowledged me. And with her, an acknowledgment always meant something.

She had this aura about her,if she caught you in the corridor, you’d hold your breath. If you were exhaling, you wouldn’t dare inhale again until she passed. That was the kind of presence she had. But beneath that formidable exterior was someone who truly believed in her students.

I remember struggling in my psychology paper. She called me in and asked, “What the hell have you done?” I admitted, “I had a blackout.” She didn’t let me off easily. “I don’t believe in blackouts, but I believe in you,” she said. And that belief changed me. I promised her I wouldn’t let her down. And when I topped my methods, she awarded me the prestigious Miss H.J Title of the year. That moment shaped my future in ways I didn’t even realise at the time.

One of the greatest compliments I’ve ever received came from her:

Personally, I see a junior Dr. Urmi Sampat in Namrata.
That comparison still humbles me.

Everything she taught me stayed with me. From my first lesson at NPKT to my journey as a teacher at Arya Vidya Mandir Bandra, to moving to Dubai , her words have never left me. The discipline, the passion, the high standards,they are woven into the way I lead today.

I wish I had the chance to say goodbye. But in a way, someone like her never truly leaves. Somewhere, I know she’s making sure everyone arrives on time, does their job well, and carries themselves with the grace and dignity she expected of us all.

Dr. Sampat, you were the epitome of grace, excellence, and discipline. They don’t make them like you anymore. I treasured you, and I always will.
Yours truly,
Namrata Simon Nayar

featured_reviews.name: Mohammed Abdul Raouf
featured_reviews.review_text:
Grant Medical College, established in 1845, is one of the oldest and most premier medical institutions in South Asia. It is consistently ranked among the top 10 medical colleges in India. Attached to the massive Sir J.J. Group of Hospitals, it serves as a tertiary care referral center for the entire state of Maharashtra.
The Strengths (Pros)
* Unmatched Clinical Exposure: This is the college's biggest selling point. The associated J.J. Hospital has a massive patient inflow (thousands of outpatients daily). As a student, you will see rare cases and common diseases in abundance. By the time you finish your internship, your clinical skills will be far superior to students from most other colleges.
* Top-Tier Faculty: The professors are often leaders in their respective fields. Being a government college in Mumbai, it attracts the best medical teachers.
* Affordability: Being a state government college, the fee structure is heavily subsidized and very affordable compared to private institutions.
* Location: Located in Byculla (South Mumbai), the campus is in the heart of the city. It is well-connected by local trains (Byculla station is walking distance) and offers access to the best of Mumbai.
* Prestige & Alumni Network: Graduating from "Grant" carries significant weight in the medical community, both in India and abroad (US/UK). The alumni network is vast and powerful.
The Challenges (Cons)
* Infrastructure & Maintenance: While the campus has beautiful heritage buildings, some facilities are aging. Lecture halls and labs are functional but may not be as modern or "glossy" as high-end private colleges.
* Hostel Conditions: This is a common complaint. Hostels can be crowded, and hygiene maintenance in the washrooms sometimes lags. Many students opt to live in PGs nearby after the first year, though this is expensive in South Mumbai.
* High Workload: The environment is high-pressure. Due to the massive patient load, internships and residency can be grueling with very long hours.
Campus Life
* Vibrant Atmosphere: The campus is huge (44 acres). It has a unique mix of medical students, nursing students, and physiotherapy students.
* Events: The annual cultural festival, "Astitva," and the sports meet, "Kurukshetra," are very popular and provide a much-needed break from studies.
* Gymkhana: There is a sprawling gymkhana ground (Marine Lines) associated with the college for sports enthusiasts.
Quick Summary Table
| Feature | Rating | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Academics | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Excellent teaching and case variety. |
| Clinical Exposure | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | World-class; arguably the best in Western India. |
| Infrastructure | ⭐⭐⭐ | Heritage buildings, but needs modernization. |
| Hostels | ⭐⭐ | Often crowded; needs renovation. |
| Fees | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ | Very economical (Govt. rates). |
Final Verdict
Grant Government Medical College is an excellent choice for students who prioritize clinical learning and hands-on experience over luxury infrastructure.
If you are willing to work hard and adjust to a heritage campus environment, this college will mold you into a highly competent doctor. It is ideal for those who want the "real" medical experience in the heart of Mumbai.
